title: The hypertrophy series: controlling volume & intensity to promote progression
summary: He argues tonnage should grow mainly by adding weight to the bar (progressive overload) rather than by piling on sets at the same weight. Extra sets eventually stop being challenging, waste time, hit cardio limits and leave no further route to progress, while heavier weight packs more tonnage into limited gym time.

claims.claim: Whether junk volume exists matters less than how you accumulate muscle damage and tonnage.
You can raise tonnage by adding sets at the same weight (e.g. another set of 9 at 200 lbs close-grip after 10 reps becomes comfortable), and on paper this can beat progressive overload.
Adding sets fails long term: you recover to baseline between sets, so the weight no longer causes meaningful fatigue, and many reps fall outside a useful intensity window.
10x10 is a poor scheme: if you can repeat 10 reps for 10 sets, most of those reps are in an uninteresting intensity window.
Intensity rises during a set, so the last rep is harder than the first, but you want all reps to count in a useful intensity window.
Adding weight to the bar makes progression easy to track; adding sets is very time-consuming and leaves no further route once exhausted.
Basing most progression on adding weight leaves room to use other methods later, such as adding sets and reps when weight increases stall.
Just adding reps at a fixed weight (e.g. snatch-grip deadlift) eventually hits cardio limits before muscular exhaustion, so people add sets to reset, which is less effective than raising the weight.

A lifter who adds 5 lbs each time they hit their rep goal will end up with more tonnage than one who stays at 300 lbs on the snatch-grip deadlift adding reps, because they fit more tonnage into less time.
Advanced lifters need more tonnage but don't get more gym time, so you must fit as much quality tonnage as possible into a limited window.
He thinks the intensity window does affect tonnage quality, but argues that either way progressive overload is the right way to balance volume and intensity.
Progressive overload raises both volume and intensity, and balancing volume and intensity improves your ability to progress; the two feed each other.
Refusing to add weight to the bar limits your ability to manipulate volume and intensity, which you need to accumulate tonnage efficiently, avoid injury and stay motivated by lifting heavy.
